claims.text: The as-synthesized nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst is a uniform multimetallic solid solution.
The as-synthesized catalyst particles are typically 5–10 nm in size.
Electrochemical cycling between approximately 0.2 and 1.0 V versus RHE promotes selective migration of Pt atoms to the catalyst surface.
Potential cycling produces a Pt-enriched surface layer relative to the bulk solid solution.
The Pt-enriched surface has modified local atomic arrangements and intrinsic strain fields.
Potential cycling preferentially oxidizes and dissolves Pd, Rh, Ru, Ir, and Os or causes those elements to migrate away from the surface.
Removal or inward migration of the non-Pt elements enriches the catalyst surface in Pt.
Pt surface enrichment changes the surface d-band center and strain state.
The altered d-band center and strain make adsorption and activation of ethanol and its intermediates more energetically favorable.
The cycled catalyst will have a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential than the as-synthesized catalyst.
The cycled catalyst will have a higher ethanol-oxidation current density than the as-synthesized catalyst.
XPS should reveal increased surface Pt content after potential cycling.
High-resolution TEM should reveal altered surface strain after potential cycling.
The proposed behavior should hold for particles around 5–10 nm under room-temperature ethanol-oxidation conditions.
The proposed mechanism should hold in either acidic or alkaline electrolyte.
Moderate potential cycling can induce surface restructuring without extensive particle sintering or bulk phase segregation.
Ligand and strain effects in related multimetallic catalyst systems support the proposed general mechanism.
